pdf.title: Thread ownership in a segmented activity kernel

sections.heading: Bug report and workspace
sections.body:
A telemetry pipeline sums active ticks per session. The device input has a row of 33 to 509 ticks per session and a row-specific cutoff length. For a batch we allocate a pitched array with a padded stride in elements. One tile is 32 consecutive lanes. The production checksum fails on sessions whose valid tail crosses a warp boundary. The failure is easier to see when two consecutive rows have unequal valid lengths. Replacing all cutoffs with the same power of two conceals it.

You receive a correct scalar CPU oracle, an intentionally faulty CUDA kernel, a Python binding and fixture arrays. Check your code against the oracle over integer values prior to profiling. The starter code hardcodes the pitch to the valid length in one helper; fixing that alone does not establish correct reduction. A heatmap of deltas can help localize incorrect rows.

sections.heading: Contract and reduced failure
sections.body: For each row r, compute one exact signed 32-bit sum of values with 0 <= j < length[r]. Padding values are deliberately large negative sentinels. No two blocks own the same output row, and no thread may read padding to obtain a convenient zero value. The host allocator pre-fills output with a nonzero pattern to reveal missing writes. The harness passes stride explicitly; do not infer stride from the number of valid values.

rows: Distinguish empty row and uninitialized write

sections.heading: Task A · Fix the kernel and prove ownership
sections.body: Write a one-paragraph map from row and tile indices to block and thread coordinates. Fix the reduction in student/segmented.cu. The baseline permits either one block per row or multiple tiles in a block. If using shared memory, specify which participating threads must reach each block barrier. A return for an invalid lane cannot silently remove that thread from a later collective. State what every inactive lane contributes before the shuffle or shared-memory step. Write a regression reproducing an intermittent failure; explain the thread schedule or visibility assumption exposed by your case.

sections.heading: Task B · Timed comparison
sections.body: The benchmark harness warms both kernels for 20 iterations, then times 60 launches on a single stream. Wait for outstanding events before reading elapsed time. Report median and p90 for row sizes 32, 33, 65 and 257. Record GPU model, compiler, block shape, version and whether the output has been verified under poison padding. Rerunning an existing sweep on the validated reference branch is a separate reporting exercise. On that branch, there is no student kernel change to make.

sections.heading: Submission checklist and grading cases
sections.body: Submit the kernel patch, one minimal failure fixture and a results table. The tests include an empty row, a tail consisting of one lane, identical adjacent rows and rows with different pitches. There is a written question about when a block-wide barrier can deadlock. A faster kernel that fails the CPU comparison receives no timing credit; a correct slow kernel still gets functional credit. Keep the raw launch measurements so that an anomalous jitter value can be inspected after the fact.
